title: Black Holes of Every Size Follow the Same Surprising Rule
summary: Black holes are famous for gobbling things up. But did you know they also burp? When a black hole tears apart a star, it doesn't swallow everything neatly. Some material gets blasted out into space in powerful jets. Now, an international team of astronomers has found something surprising: black holes of all sizes — from small ones about 10 times the mass of our sun to supermassive ones millions of times heavier — launch these jets at the same point in their feeding cycle. How did they figure that out? They watched tidal disruption events (TDEs). That's when a star wanders too close to a supermassive black hole and gets ripped apart by gravity. After that, the black hole suddenly has a big meal to eat. Normally, changes around supermassive black holes take thousands or millions of years. But TDEs let astronomers see the action unfold in just a few years. The team studied 20 TDEs using telescopes in America, Australia, India, South Africa, and space. They narrowed it down to 10 good ones. They found two separate times when jets can form. The second one happens hundreds to thousands of days after the star is destroyed. At that point, the black hole's feeding rate drops to about 2% of its Eddington limit — the balance point between gravity pulling in and radiation pushing out. That same 2% threshold already triggers jets in much smaller black holes. Why does it matter? It suggests that this part of black hole physics works the same way across an enormous range of sizes. One rule, many black holes.
why_it_matters: It shows how scientists look for patterns that work for both tiny and gigantic things — just like one math rule can solve a small problem and a huge one, once you spot it.

keywords.explanation: An object in space with gravity so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape it.
Powerful streams of material that get blasted out into space.
Extremely huge — a supermassive black hole can be millions of times heavier than our sun.
When a star wanders too close to a supermassive black hole and gets ripped apart by gravity.

questions.question: Besides gobbling things up, what do black holes also do?
options: They stop time around them
They shine like normal stars
They turn into planets
They burp, blasting some material out into space
questions.correct_answer: They burp, blasting some material out into space

questions.question: What is a tidal disruption event (TDE)?
options: When a star is born inside a black hole
When a star wanders too close to a supermassive black hole and gets ripped apart
When two black holes crash into each other
When a black hole stops eating for a year
questions.correct_answer: When a star wanders too close to a supermassive black hole and gets ripped apart

questions.question: Why do TDEs help astronomers?
options: They let astronomers watch changes unfold in just a few years instead of thousands or millions of years
They make telescopes work faster
They happen every night near Earth
They make black holes easy to see with your eyes
questions.correct_answer: They let astronomers watch changes unfold in just a few years instead of thousands or millions of years

options: Exactly one day after the star arrives

background_read: Black holes form when very huge stars run out of fuel and collapse. Most big galaxies, including our own Milky Way, have a supermassive black hole sitting quietly at the center.
In 2019, astronomers used telescopes all around the world together to take the first-ever picture of a black hole's shadow — proof that teamwork across countries really works in science.
Scientists use a number called the Eddington limit to compare black holes of very different sizes, a bit like comparing small and big engines by how hard they are working.
Article_Structure: WHO: An international team of astronomers studying black holes of all sizes
WHAT: They found that black holes from small ones to supermassive ones launch jets at the same point in their feeding cycle, around 2% of the Eddington limit
WHERE: Telescopes in America, Australia, India, South Africa and in space
WHY: It suggests one rule of black hole physics works the same way across an enormous range of sizes — one rule, many black holes

perspectives.description: They are excited because the same rule seems to work for tiny black holes and giant ones, which makes the universe look simpler than expected.
Some may point out the team started with 20 TDEs and used only 10, so more observations are needed before calling it a universal rule.
Better telescopes could catch more TDEs and test whether the 2% jet trigger really happens everywhere in the universe.
